name: Kanite
confidence_why: Young 1962 describes Kanite as having a single contrastive high tone whose position distinguishes minimal pairs, with stress always falling on the high-tone syllable, and Gibson and McCarthy's 1992 phonology data sheet agrees (two phonemic tones, stress on the high tone); the only divergence is a footnote in McCarthy 1965 calling the same prominence "phonemic stress" of low functional load, a naming difference the same authors later abandoned in favour of tone, so the record rests on two first-hand descriptions that agree on the type.
catalog_citation: Young, Rosemary. 1962. The phonemes of Kanite, Kamano, Benabena, and Gahuku. In James C. Dean (ed.), Studies in New Guinea linguistics by members of the Summer Institute of Linguistics (New Guinea Branch), 90-110. Oceania Linguistic Monographs 6. Sydney: University of Sydney. [Rosetta Project excerpt, archive.org item = pp. 93-99]
catalog_quote: In these four languages the contrastive supra-segmental feature is not so much one of pitch levels or stress intensity as of syllable emphasis. That is, each language has one distinct supra-segmental phoneme which when it occurs gives contrast to affected syllables over neutral syllables. In KANITE and GAHUKU it is a phoneme of tone, which has been described as high tone and which contrasts with syllables which may be described as being either low tone or toneless. Minimal word pairs contrast as to the syllables on which the tone is placed. Examples: ... KANITE ke'na "skirt" 'ke'na "bamboo" ... In KAMANO and BENABENA it is a phoneme of stress which contrasts with syllables which are unstressed. ... [p. 99] In KANITE and GAHUKU tone occurs on both nouns and verbs. ... in KANITE there are no toneless (completely low tone) words, the only examples being nouns which form part of a compound verb expression and which are therefore bound to the verb stem. The tone on nouns in KANITE is perturbed by the preceding adjective, determined by the class of the adjective and the vowel of the initial syllable of the noun. No such perturbation occurs between adjacent nouns and verbs however. In KANITE also, high tone and stress always occur on the same syllable.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kanite has no positionally fixed word stress: the single contrastive suprasegmental is a lexically placed high tone (vs low/toneless syllables), with minimal pairs differing only in which syllable carries it; stress (intensity) always falls on the high-toned syllable(s). Every word has at least one high tone; a noun's tone is perturbed by a preceding adjective (conditioned by adjective class and the noun's initial-syllable vowel). The later SIL Organised Phonology Data (Gibson & McCarthy, 1992/2004, p.3) restates: 'Stress occurs on high tone. Kanite has two phonemic tones.'; McCarthy 1965 fn.: 'Stress is phonemic but carries a low functional load.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said for Kanite (words may carry more than one high tone, e.g. tʌ'ʔe'ne 'our teeth'); Young describes secondary/second stress only for Kamano and Benabena.
new_statements.exceptions: No toneless words except nouns bound into compound verb expressions; noun tone perturbed (sandhi) after adjectives; no perturbation between adjacent nouns and verbs.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level phonemic description based on isolated words and minimal pairs; tone sandhi noted at the adjective+noun phrase level. OPD describes the Kemeyu Kanite variety.
new_statements.identity_note: Young 1962 describes Kanite proper (fieldwork by Gibson & McCarthy from 1957 in a Kanite village); the 1992/2004 OPD is headed 'Kanite (Kemeyu Kanite)', villages Kemeyu, Anupalu, Ko'kopi, Kuana (Okapa district). The grammar sketch also carries notes on Inoke (= Inoke-Yate, ISO ino, glottocode inok1238, a separate Glottolog language) and the Kagufi sub-dialect; the stress/tone statements quoted do not concern those.

readall_conflicts: No new source was read, so nothing new conflicts. 3.3 (pp. 98-99) treats the contrastive suprasegmental as syllable emphasis rather than pitch or intensity, the Organised Phonology Data sheet p. 3 says 'Stress occurs on high tone. Kanite has two phonemic tones.' (stress predictable from tone), while the grammar-sketch reprint of McCarthy 1965 (p. 115 fn.) says 'Stress is phonemic but carries a low functional load' — a mild difference in whether stress or tone is the underlying contrast, already noted; none of these gives a positional stress rule.

tone.quote: The Eastern New Guinea Highlands group tends to have tonal languages, such as Gadsup, Binumarien, Siane, Awa, Kanite, etc. which may contrast tone on any syllable (see McKaughan [1973] for several of these). ... Some languages seem to require a High tone in a word (Narak, Kairi, Kanite, Awad Bing, etc.).
